description: A much-branched, slightly spiny shrub 2-4 m tall with small opposite lanceolate leaves, clusters of tiny fragrant white to pinkish flowers and small round brownish fruits. Dried, powdered leaves yield a reddish-orange dye.
cultural_significance: Mehendi designs are applied to the hands and feet of brides and on festivals such as Karva Chauth, Eid and Teej across South Asia. The dye is a symbol of auspiciousness and joy. Not a Vedic-era plant by name; prominent in later Nighantus and Unani texts.
habitat: Hot, dry tropical and subtropical regions; grown as hedges and field crops, especially in Rajasthan (Sojat) and Gujarat.

uses.title: Hair conditioning and dye
uses.detail: Leaf powder paste is a traditional natural hair dye and conditioner, used to reduce dandruff and cool the scalp.

uses.title: Skin and wound care
uses.detail: Leaf paste is traditionally applied to burns, boils and inflammation as a cooling Vranaropana application.

uses.title: Cooling for the body
uses.detail: Palm and sole application is traditionally believed to cool the body in summer, and in Unani practice the leaf paste is used for headaches.

uses.title: Mouth and throat gargle
uses.detail: Leaf decoction is used as a gargle for mouth ulcers and sore throat in folk practice.

preparations.name: Henna paste
preparations.method: Mix dried leaf powder with lemon water or tea and rest for several hours until the dye is released; apply and leave on for hours before washing.
preparations.note: For skin or hair; do a patch test.

preparations.name: Hair mask
preparations.method: Mix henna with curd or amla powder and apply to the scalp and hair.

preparations.name: Leaf decoction
preparations.method: Boil leaves in water, cool and use as a gargle or wound wash.

preparations.name: Henna flower oil
preparations.method: Flowers soaked or boiled in oil, used for fragrance and head cooling.

precautions: Pure natural henna is generally safe on skin, but 'black henna' sold for temporary tattoos contains PPD (para-phenylenediamine), which can cause severe allergic reactions and scarring. People with G6PD deficiency should avoid henna, especially on infants, because of a risk of haemolysis. Do a patch test. Internal use of leaf or bark is not advised without guidance and is avoided in pregnancy.

cultivation.soil: Well-drained sandy loam; tolerates poor and saline soil
cultivation.harvest: Leaves are harvested 2-3 times a year and dried in shade

fun_fact: The dye molecule lawsone binds to the keratin in skin and hair, which is why mehendi stains last for one to three weeks.

regions.name: Rajasthan (Thar Desert)
regions.note: Sojat is a major henna-growing area

regions.name: Iran & Central Asia
regions.note: Used for hair and skin dye
